Simulation study · extreme value estimation

The Composite Expectile Estimator

Fitting an extreme value distribution by an expectile loss integrated against a tail-weighted measure, so that a misspecified body does not compromise the tail. Against maximum likelihood, L-moments, and the composite quantile estimator on a Gaussian-contaminated GEV; and, in its strongest form — a GPD fitted this way and smooth grafted onto an empirical body — against peaks-over-threshold, which it beats at every return period from 50 to 1000 years.

2000 Monte Carlo replicates · n = 50, 100, 200 Truth: max(GEV, Normal) All code and outputs reproducible

What the experiment found

Confirmed

L2 fixes the variance explosion. At matched weight, the composite expectile estimator's mean squared error for the 1000-year return level is 0.17–0.58× that of the composite quantile estimator — a two- to six-fold improvement, at every weight tested. The L1 version's far-tail standard deviation is roughly double the L2 version's.

Confirmed

Both remove the bias. Maximum likelihood and L-moments underestimate the 1000-year return level by 39% and 32% asymptotically under this contamination. Both composite estimators cut that to under 1%.

Qualified

The weight was starting too late. With the weight switching on near the median rather than at the 95th percentile, the composite expectile estimator matches the GEV MLE on MSE from T = 200 to T = 1000 (ratios 0.98 to 1.05, all within Monte Carlo error of 1) while carrying a quarter of its bias. In this contamination setting it never significantly beats it — but see below.

New obstacle

Expectiles are anchored to the mean, so body contamination never fully leaves them. No weight function makes the L2 version asymptotically unbiased, whereas the L1 version is exactly unbiased. And the raw L2 criterion is infinite once ξ ≥ 1/2 — precisely the heavy-tailed regime the method exists to serve.

New

Mixing the two losses helps. A convex combination of the check functions elicits an intermediate functional — the α-elastile. Its contamination, bias and variance all interpolate smoothly, and an interior α beats both pure losses by 5 to 23% on MSE at every return period up to 500. The best α rises with the return period.

Closed off

The mean anchoring can be removed exactly, and it is not worth it. Taking the mean from the data instead of the model cuts the surviving contamination at p = 0.98 from 9.73% to 0.0001% and puts the asymptotic target on the true parameters — but the sample mean is too noisy at n = 100, and the corrected estimator loses on every finite-sample criterion.

Best result

Against what a practitioner would actually do, the composite version wins. A GPD fitted by the composite L2 criterion with a convex weight and smooth grafted onto an empirical body beats peaks-over-threshold at every return period from 50 to 1000, on MSE, on median error, and on head-to-head win rate. But most of that margin is not the loss function — see the next line.

Qualified hard

Two thirds of that headline gain survives when nothing is misspecified. Repeating the comparison on data that really are iid GPD, the same estimator still beats the same POT–MLE(0.90) reference by a ratio of 0.344 at T = 1000, against 0.209 on the contaminated truth. On a log scale, 68% of the gain is present with a perfect model and only 32% comes from the misspecification the method exists to exploit. The reference keeps ten exceedances out of a hundred observations, and against a real efficiency bound it is 2.58× worse at T = 1000 even when correctly specified.

The premium

On a correctly specified GEV the composite estimators cost 12–32% in the far tail and 2–3.7× in the body — but on a correctly specified GPD they cost nothing in the far tail, reaching 0.63 against the MLE at T = 1000. The premium is not a single number; it depends on the fitting setup, and in both settings the cost sits at short return periods. In both, the estimators under-predict — the unsafe direction for design.

And

Grafting onto an empirical body fixes the rest. Used as the tail of a smooth graft with the empirical distribution as the body, the composite expectile fit goes from 1168× the MLE's error at the 2-year level to 1.15×, and beats the MLE across the whole tail (0.82× at T = 200, 0.84× at T = 1000, closer on 80% of datasets). Grafting the MLE onto the same body gains nothing, so it is the composite tail doing the work.

And

There is a realistic setting where L2 wins outright. When the body is near-degenerate — ordinary snowmelt maxima clustered tightly, a heavy rain-on-snow tail — the composite expectile estimator's typical error at the 1000-year level is 0.58× the MLE's, and it is the closer of the two on 84% of datasets. The composite quantile estimator is worse than the MLE there, winning 38%.

The competitor

Fung's weighted likelihood wins the GEV comparison and loses the GPD one. MWLE tilts the likelihood rather than the loss, and on a three-parameter GEV it takes the best far-tail number here (0.86× the MLE under contamination) while paying only 4–5% when the model is right, against 12–32% for the composites. On a two-parameter GPD above a known threshold it buys nothing — 0.99 to 1.03 — where the inverted Huber reaches 0.63. The peaks-over-threshold setting is the one flood practice uses.

Handover, unresolved

The handover weight w = p⁶ is a poor one. A plain hard graft at the 0.90- or 0.95-quantile matches or beats it at every return period (0.16 against 0.18 at T = 1000). But the hard graft is the step member of the smooth-graft family, and the run swept the join over five values while holding the handover weight at one, so it does not compare the two constructions — it compares five members of a family against one other member, and finds the one wanting. That w(0.9) = 0.531 gives the tail model majority share at the ten-year level says the fix is a sharper handover weight, not a hard join. Deferred to the graft work.

Free lunch

The extremile version costs nothing at all. Matching the extremile function instead of a loss gives a tail-weighted probability-weighted-moment estimator that, at a short reach, sits at the MLE in the body (0.98 at T = 2) and takes 26% off the far-tail MSE, beating L-moments throughout. It does not reach the M-estimator composites' gains under contamination, but it is a strictly better default than L-moments.

01The estimator, and a correction to the loss

The proposal is to fit a parametric family indexed by θ by minimising an expectile loss integrated over levels, against a weight that is zero on the body of the distribution and rises towards one in the tail:

S(θ) = Σ i ∫ 01 w(p) |p − I(y i < E(p|θ))| (y i − E(p|θ))2 dp

where E(·|θ) is the family's expectile function. The reasoning is that a named parametric family is essentially always misspecified, and a global fitting criterion — likelihood, L-moments — has to spread that misspecification across the whole distribution. If only the tail matters, weighting the criterion towards the tail should buy a better tail fit. The same construction with the pinball loss and the quantile function is the composite quantile estimator; the question here is whether replacing L1 by L2 tames the variance explosion that made the L1 version not worth using.

The absolute value marked in red is necessary and was missing from the proposal as stated. Without it the factor (p − I) is negative for every observation below E, so pushing E upward sends the criterion to −∞; minimising it numerically simply runs to whatever boundary the optimiser is given. The ordering (y − E) is correct as written — it is squared, so it does not matter — and the indicator I(y < E) is correct too. The pinball loss (p − I(y < q))(y − q) takes no absolute value and is already non-negative, which is presumably where the slip came from.

With the absolute value, each integrand is the canonical strictly consistent scoring function for its functional, so the integrated loss is minimised in expectation by a θ whose expectile (respectively quantile) function matches the truth wherever w > 0.

02The simulation design

The truth is a Gaussian-contaminated GEV: the distribution of max(X, Z) with X ~ GEV and Z ~ Normal independent, so its cdf is the product

F(x) = F GEV(x; 0, 1, 0.2) · Φ((x − 1.5) / 0.8)

The normal sits in the middle: it dominates the body and vanishes in the tail, so the GEV is the exactly correct tail model and a wrong body model. That is the situation the tail-focused idea is built for.

It is worth looking at what this actually does, because on a return-period axis the contamination looks smaller than it is. On the quantile scale the two curves have converged by about T = 15; the damage is all in the body, below the 90th percentile, where the truth's median is 4.6× its GEV component's and its mean is 2.4×. That body is exactly what likelihood and L-moments spend their fit on.

The second row is the alternative setting suggested as a check, GEV(23, 22.2, 0.39) against N(61.9, 16.9). It has a much heavier tail but, on the quantile scale, milder contamination: 2.5% at T = 10 against 11% here, and a mean ratio of 1.6 against 2.4. The setting used throughout is the more contaminated of the two.

The weight function

A smoothstep, zero below p₀ and one above p₁. The primary design used p₀ = 0.95 and p₁ = 0.98, placed where the quantile contamination dies out (it leaves the quantiles 0.6% too high at p₀ and 0.00003% at p₁). Section 6 shows this choice, principled for L1, is badly wrong for L2, and section 5 sweeps it.

Estimators and reporting

GEV by maximum likelihood; GEV by L-moments (Hosking); composite quantile (L1); composite expectile (L2). 2000 replicates at n = 50, 100 and 200, all four estimators fitted to identical datasets, so every comparison below can be made paired — which matters, because the sampling distribution of a far-tail return level is heavy-tailed and unpaired Monte Carlo error would swamp the differences at issue. Every ratio quoted carries a paired Monte Carlo standard error. The shape parameter is bounded to [−0.45, 0.90] for all four estimators alike.

03Expectiles are anchored to the mean

This is the finding that most constrains the idea, and it is specific to L2.

The p-quantile of the contaminated truth equals the p-quantile of its GEV component as soon as the normal's cdf reaches one. Quantiles are tail-local. Expectiles are not. The p-expectile solves

k · φ(x) + m − x = 0, k = (2p − 1)/(1 − p), φ(x) = E[(Y − x)+]

and while φ(x) for large x sees only the tail, the mean m sees everything — including the contaminated body. So the truth's expectiles differ from its GEV component's at every level, by an amount that decays only like (1 − p)ξ.

How much of the body contamination is still present in each functional. The quantile discrepancy reaches machine precision by the 50-year level; the expectile discrepancy is still 9.7% there, and 1.4% at 10 000 years.

04Return levels, and the price of unbiasedness

Bias is only half the account. The panels below show the sampling distribution of each estimator's return-level curve at n = 100, under the primary weight.

Maximum likelihood has a tight band whose centre flattens badly below the truth — the 20–40% bias of the previous section, visible as a curve that stops rising. The composite estimators track the truth far better in the median and pay for it in width. The two lower-right panels use a weight capped so that it does not extend past the largest observation (section 6); the capped L1 median follows the truth almost exactly to T = 1000, with a 95% band running from 5 to beyond 30.

On mean squared error, at this weight, no composite design beats maximum likelihood anywhere from T = 20 to T = 1000. The trade each makes against the MLE at T = 1000, in MSE units, is the compact way to see why:

05How much is the tail focus, and how much is L1 versus L2?

The previous section fixes the weight at one setting, which conflates two things: the choice of functional and the strength of the tail focus. Sweeping the lower edge p₀ from 0 (w ≡ 1, no tail focus at all) up to 0.95 separates them. At p₀ = 0 the composite quantile estimator is exactly CRPS minimisation, which is the like-for-like benchmark against L-moments: both are global, quantile-flavoured, and neither has any tail focus.

The two panels behave completely differently in the far tail. Every L2 curve converges to roughly 1.05 at T = 1000 whatever the weight; every L1 curve diverges upward, the worst of them to 6× the MLE. That contrast is the answer to the original question.

Paired comparison of the two losses at matched weight, same 2000 datasets: MSE(L2) / MSE(L1) for the 1000-year return level, with the Monte Carlo standard error of the paired difference. L2 wins decisively at every weight.

Two things stand out. First, L2's far-tail standard deviation is almost invariant to the weight (5.8 to 6.7 across the whole sweep) while L1's swings between 4.3 and 15.0. The expectile criterion is simply a much better conditioned thing to minimise under tail weighting, because expectiles are smooth functionals of the whole sample while quantiles lean on a handful of order statistics.

Second, the sign of the comparison flips at p₀ = 0. With no tail focus, the quantile version has the lower variance (ratio 0.83 in L2's favour on MSE, but sd 4.32 against 6.72 — L2 wins on MSE there only through bias). So the L2 advantage is not a general property of expectiles; it is specific to tail-weighted criteria, which is exactly where the proposal lives.

Where the weight should start

The primary design put p₀ at 0.95, where the quantile contamination dies out. That is correct reasoning for L1 and wrong for L2 — section 3 showed the expectile contamination is still 16% there, so restricting to the extreme tail costs a great deal of data and buys almost no bias reduction. Worth noting

An estimator that ties on MSE but recovers ξ correctly is not the same product as one that wins on MSE. If what a study needs is a defensible shape parameter and a return-level curve that does not flatten, that is a different and possibly more useful thing than a marginally smaller squared error.

06When is the family wrong enough for this to win?

Everything so far says the tail-focused estimators tie the MLE at best. The natural next question is whether that is a property of the method or of the test: is there a realistic truth whose tail bias is severe enough that a global fit must lose? Two attempts, one that failed instructively and one that worked.

Making the family more wrong does not help by itself

The first attempt replaces max(GEV, Normal) with a graft: above a join level the truth IS the GEV, exactly, and below it the body is a different distribution carrying no information about the tail at all. That removes the leak in the max construction, where the GEV component still shapes the upper body and so hands a global fit some tail information for free. Hydrologically it is the standard mixed-population picture, and it fits the rain-on-snow story directly: in most years the annual maximum is an ordinary snowmelt peak from a much less variable process, and in the rest it is a rain-on-snow event from a genuinely heavy-tailed one.

With GEV(0, 1, 0.4) above the 90th percentile and a truncated normal below, maximum likelihood is 55% low at the 1000-year level — far worse than the 39% in the main setting. And every composite estimator does worse against it, not better: MSE ratios of 2.8 to 4.5 at T = 1000. The reason is that the heavier tail which inflates the MLE's bias inflates the composite estimators' variance at the same time. Their standard deviation at T = 1000 is 35 to 45 on a true return level of 37.

The governing ratio

To first order the fractional return-level error at large T behaves like log(T) times the error in ξ. So the contest is decided not by the size of the MLE's bias but by (ξtrue − ξMLE) / sd(ξ̂composite) — and that ratio is roughly constant in T, which is exactly why the MSE-ratio curves flatten out in the far tail. Heavier tails move both terms together. What is needed is a truth that drags the global fit's shape hard while leaving a large, clean region for the weighted criterion to read.

A near-degenerate body does

The second attempt keeps the max construction and simply makes the normal much tighter and higher: max(GEV(0, 1, 0.2), N(2.5, 0.3)). Physically this is the sharper version of the same story — ordinary snowmelt maxima cluster tightly because they are set by a fairly repeatable snowpack, and the heavy tail is entirely rain-on-snow. Statistically it drags a global fit hard (the MLE converges to σ = 0.39 against a true 1, and is 49% low at the 1000-year level) while leaving every level above the median GEV-governed, so a tail-weighted criterion gets a clean and precise read: sd(ξ̂) = 0.099 for the expectile version.

Here the composite expectile estimator wins, and the composite quantile estimator does not:

On typical error the composite expectile estimator is 40% closer to the truth than the MLE at every return period from 100 to 1000, and it is the closer of the two on 84% of datasets at T = 1000. The composite quantile estimator does not share this at all — at T = 1000 it is worse than the MLE on the same criterion, winning only 38% of the time. So this setting cleanly separates the two losses, in L2's favour, in exactly the way the original hypothesis predicted.

Mean squared error is the one criterion that still calls it a tie at T = 1000 (1.10 ± 0.28). That is not a contradiction: the expectile estimator's error distribution has a small proportion of very poor replicates, and squared error is dominated by them. Which summary matters depends on whether an occasional large overestimate of a design flood is worse than a systematic underestimate of every one — and in flood frequency it usually is not.

07Which weight functions are admissible

The weight cannot be chosen freely, and there are two separate conditions — one on the weight, one on the distribution being fitted.

The condition on the weight

Writing u = 1 − p, the population risk at level p decays as

quantile (L1): r p ~ u1 − ξ expectile (L2): r p ~ u1 − 2ξ

with the measured log-log slopes converging to these to three decimals as u → 0. So for a weight that blows up like w(p) ~ (1 − p)−a, the criterion is finite if and only if

quantile (L1): a < 2 − ξ expectile (L2): a < 2 − 2ξ

At ξ = 0.2 that is a < 1.8 and a < 1.6, so a weight going like 1/(1 − p) is admissible for both and 1/(1 − p)² for neither. Note the L2 threshold is the tighter of the two. Taking the worst case over the range where the quantile version is defined at all, ξ ↑ 1, gives a < 1 — which reproduces the L1 result reported in the original thesis work.

The weight used throughout this study is bounded — identically 0 below p₀ and identically 1 above p₁ — so it clears both conditions with room to spare at every shape the estimators visit. Nothing here requires a weight bounded by 1; that is simply what was used.

The condition on the distribution — and this one separates L1 from L2

The quantile risk needs only a finite first moment, ξ < 1. The expectile risk needs a finite second moment, ξ < 1/2, because E[(e − Y)² 1{Y < e}] is infinite for every e once the variance is:

Population risk at p = 0.99 for a GEV truth, by shape parameter.

No weight function repairs this — the criterion is +∞ at every θ. So the L2 version, taken literally, is undefined exactly in the heavy-tailed regime the method exists to serve. For flood frequency that is not a remote corner of the parameter space: the alternative setting examined here has ξ = 0.39.

The repair is standard: minimise the loss difference against a fixed reference function,

Σ i ∫ w(p) [ ρ p(y i, T(p|θ)) − ρ p(y i, T ref(p)) ] dp

which has the same minimiser and is finite whenever E|Y| < ∞. In this study ξ = 0.2, so the raw criterion is finite and nothing was needed — but it should be built in before the estimator meets anything heavier.

The same condition, across every method here

The moment requirement is not peculiar to the composite estimators. But it splits into three different questions that are easy to run together, and running them together gives the wrong answer. Is the raw criterion finite? Is the target functional even defined? And does the estimator have the usual root-n limit? Each is a different power of the tail.

Write the loss as ρp,a(y, t) = |p − I(y < t)| |y − t|a. The raw criterion needs E|Y|a. But the loss difference above is bounded by C(1 + |Y|a−1), and so is the estimating equation it differentiates to,

p E[(Y − t)a−1; Y > t] = (1 − p) E[(t − Y)a−1; Y < t]

so the functional is defined under E|Y|a−1 < ∞ — one order cheaper. Squaring that score for the sandwich meat gives E|Y|2(a−1) for the root-n limit. Reading the three off a GPD tail with index 1/ξ:

The exponent a is the power in the loss: a = 1 is the pinball, a = 2 the asymmetric square, and intermediate a gives the La-quantiles of section 14. Only the middle column decides whether the target exists; the first is repaired for free by the loss-difference form.

Three things fall out. First, the quantile needs nothing: the raw ξ < 1 in its first column is an artefact of not recentring, and the pinball functional is defined for any tail at all. Second, the α-elastile buys no domain. It is a sum, finite only if both terms are, so every α above zero inherits the expectile's ξ < 1/2 for the root-n limit — mixing trades bias against variance inside that domain and cannot widen it. Third, and the reason the La family is worth its own experiment rather than being folded into the elastile: it is the only continuous path off L1 that does widen the domain. At a = 1.5 the functional survives to ξ < 2 and the root-n limit to ξ < 1, against ξ < 1 and ξ < 1/2 for L2. So a is a dial on how much tail heaviness the method tolerates, and α is not.

L-moments and L2 have the same domain

Worth noting for the practitioner comparison: probability-weighted moment estimators are consistent for ξ < 1 and asymptotically normal only for ξ < 1/2 — exactly the composite expectile's two thresholds. Whatever else switching from L-moments to L2 costs, it costs nothing in admissible tail heaviness. The comparison in section 13 is like-for-like on this axis.

A third trap: weight beyond the data

A weight left at one all the way to p = 1 puts a large share of its mass at levels above the largest observation. Out there the empirical quantile and expectile functions have both saturated at the sample maximum, so the loss can only pull the fitted tail down. The fitted shape parameter tracks that share almost exactly:

At n = 50 this pins 89% of L1 fits and 56% of L2 fits onto the shape bound. Capping the weight at p = 1 − 1/n fixes the shape (median ξ̂ moves from −0.26 to 0.19 for L1 and −0.20 to 0.06 for L2) — but for L1 it then worsens the far-tail MSE by an order of magnitude, because the downward drag had been acting as accidental shrinkage. L2 survives capping intact. Whatever else is done with the estimator, the weight should not extend past where the data can speak.

08Mixing the two losses: the α-elastile

The two losses fail in opposite directions — L1 unbiased and wild, L2 steadier and slightly biased — which invites an elastic-net-style compromise. Taking a convex combination of the two check functions at the same level,

ραp(y, t) = (α/s) |p − I(y < t)| (y − t)2 + (1 − α) (p − I(y < t)) (y − t)

gives a strictly consistent scoring function for a new functional — the α-elastile. Differentiating the expected loss identifies it as the unique root of

G(t) = (2α/s) [ (1 − 2p) φ(t) + (1 − p)(t − m) ] + (1 − α) [ F(t) − p ] = 0

The first bracket vanishes at the expectile, the second at the quantile, and both are increasing in t — so G is strictly increasing, the root is unique, and it always lies between the quantile and the expectile, which makes for a perfect bracket in the solver. α = 0 recovers the quantile and α = 1 the expectile.

The scale s carries units of y and is what makes α = 1/2 mean anything: without it the L2 term is in units of y² and the L1 term in units of y. It is fixed per dataset at the ratio of the two integrated losses evaluated at a preliminary L-moment fit, so the two contribute equally there. Being constant during the optimisation, it does not disturb the properness of the criterion; it only chooses the units in which α interpolates.

The contamination interpolates smoothly

The reason to expect the mixture to help is that the structural obstacle of section 3 arrives gradually. The percentage by which the truth's functional exceeds its GEV component's — the contamination no weight can remove — runs smoothly from the quantile's zero to the expectile's:

Mixing helps, by 5 to 23% over whichever pure loss is better, and the optimal α rises with the return period — from about 0.1 at T = 10 to pure L2 at T = 1000. That is the elastic-net pattern, and it has a clean reading here: the further out you extrapolate, the more the variance term dominates and the more of the expectile's smoothing you want.

Two caveats. The benefit depends on the weight being well placed: repeating the sweep at p₀ = 0.95 gives an interior optimum only at T ≤ 20, and the pure losses win everywhere beyond. And α is a tuning parameter, so a fair account of it needs the selection cost folded in — these are oracle values.

09Grafting the composite fit onto an empirical body

Everything above reports the composite fit as if it were the whole distribution, which is unfair to it and unlike how it would be used. The estimator buys its tail by abandoning the body, and the damage is severe: at p₀ = 0.95 the mean squared error of the 2-year return level is eleven thousand times the MLE's for the quantile version and a thousand times for the expectile version. That is not a subtlety, it is a ruined distribution.

The natural repair is to use the composite fit only as the tail of a smooth graft whose body is the empirical distribution. The construction used here is the hazard-mixture smooth graft (Coia and De Michele), taken from probaverse/distplyr rather than reimplemented, which mixes body and tail on the hazard rather than the density and so has no jump or kink at the handover and no normalising constant. Writing w for the handover weight and M = (1-w) Sbody + w Stail, the survival is S = M C with a correction factor C driven by w'.

With a weight that is exactly 0 below xlo and exactly 1 above xhi, the construction collapses to three regimes, which is worth spelling out because it explains the results:

  • below xlo: w' = 0 so C = 1, and the graft is the empirical distribution;
  • between: the transition, the only part needing the integral;
  • above xhi: w' = 0 again, so C freezes at a constant c and S(x) = c · Stail(x) — the fitted tail, rescaled by a single constant that reconciles it with the body's mass at the handover.

That last point matters: the graft does not merely paste the fitted tail on, it re-anchors it. So one should expect the body to be fixed by construction, and the tail to change too.

Both expectations hold. The handover weight was run two ways — the same weight used in the fitting criterion, as proposed, and a fixed [0.90, 0.98] window — because the two weights do different jobs: one says which levels to fit, the other says where to stop trusting the data.

The body is completely repaired. Eleven thousand becomes 1.15, which is the empirical distribution's own figure — as it must be, since below the handover the graft is exactly the empirical distribution. The composite estimator's worst liability simply disappears.

The tail improves as well, which was not guaranteed. The best combination, composite expectile fitted at p₀ = 0.5 and handed over on [0.90, 0.98], beats the GEV MLE at every return period from 50 to 1000 — 0.92, 0.82, 0.80, 0.84 — each five to eight standard errors below one, and it is closer to the truth than the MLE on 80% of datasets. Ungrafted, the same fit was 1.07, 0.98, 0.98, 1.05: a tie. The re-anchoring constant c is doing real work.

The control settles it

Grafting the MLE onto the same empirical body gives 1.13, 1.07, 1.03, 1.02 and a 50% win rate — that is, nothing. Grafting L-moments is likewise neutral. So the gain is not the empirical body, and it is not the graft; it is the composite expectile tail, which only becomes usable once the graft takes the body off its hands. Neither ingredient works alone.

Two practical points. The handover weight should not be tied to the fitting weight: handing over at [0.50, 0.53] because the criterion was fitted from p₀ = 0.5 means trusting the parametric model from the 53rd percentile up, and costs a factor of 1.6 at T = 1000 against the decoupled [0.90, 0.98] version. And the graft does not rescue the L1 fit — grafted, the composite quantile estimator is still 6.4× the MLE at T = 1000. The tail model has to be worth grafting.

10Fixing the mean anchoring: it works, and it does not pay

Section 3 identified the one structural disadvantage L2 carries against L1: the expectile is anchored to the distribution's mean, so body contamination never fully leaves it. The identification equation splits cleanly, though —

k φ(x) + m − x = 0

— into a tail-local part (the partial moment φ, where a GEV fitted to a contaminated sample is right) and a global part (the mean, where it is not). So take the second from the data: replace the model's mean by the sample mean and leave φ as the model's. The mean becomes a nuisance parameter profiled out nonparametrically.

As a piece of statistics it works exactly as designed. The contamination surviving in the expectile at p = 0.98 falls from 9.73% to 0.0001%, and the estimator's asymptotic target moves onto the true tail parameters:

Asymptotic targets, fitted to a sample of 2×106. The true tail is (0, 1, 0.20).
estimatorμσξbias at T = 100at T = 1000
Composite expectile, p₀ = 0.950.8360.8720.220+2.86%+0.51%
  → mean-anchored0.0260.9890.202−0.32%−0.23%
Composite expectile, p₀ = 0.901.0060.7970.237+1.22%+0.25%
  → mean-anchored0.1610.9530.208−0.49%−0.26%

The structural obstacle is gone: anchored, the L2 estimator is as asymptotically unbiased as L1.

And yet it is worse

At n = 100 the correction loses on every criterion at every return period. The median fitted shape goes from 0.209 (ordinary, p₀ = 0.5) to 0.079, and at p₀ = 0.95 it collapses to −0.45, the shape bound. Mean squared error at T = 1000 goes from 1.05 to 1.09 relative to the MLE; median absolute error from 4.68 to 4.81; the head-to-head win rate from 78% to 76%. Grafted, the ordinary version still wins (0.84× the MLE against 0.92×).

The reason is visible in the equation. An error δ in the anchor moves the solution by about δ/(1 + k S(x)), which for large p is essentially δ itself — the whole expectile curve translates by the sample mean's estimation error. Under a contaminated, heavy-tailed truth at n = 100 that error is not small, and it is injected at every level. Worse, the criterion must now reconcile a data-driven anchor with a model-driven φ, and when the weight is confined to the tail the model has little left to adjust except the shape — which is why ξ̂ is driven to its bound.

So this is a clean negative result, and it closes off the direction rather than opening it: the mean anchoring is real, the fix removes it exactly, and the fix is not worth its variance. If the idea is to be revived it needs a low-variance estimate of the anchor — a shrunk or model-averaged mean, or the mean of a trimmed body — not the raw sample mean.

11Where the handover should sit

Section 9 used a fixed [0.90, 0.98] handover on the grounds that the fitting weight and the handover weight do different jobs. Sweeping it further out tests that: if the empirical body is good, handing over later should be better.

It is not. Later is monotonically worse:

Composite expectile fitted at p₀ = 0.5, grafted onto an empirical body with the handover swept. MSE relative to the GEV MLE, n = 100, 2000 replicates, paired standard errors.
handoverT = 20T = 50T = 100T = 200T = 500T = 1000
0.90 – 0.981.471.280.92 ±0.020.82 ±0.020.80 ±0.030.84 ±0.03
0.95 – 0.991.791.711.161.000.951.00 ±0.04
0.97 – 0.9951.791.941.431.811.832.00 ±0.13
0.99 – 0.9991.791.931.812.332.322.51 ±0.18

The mechanism is the empirical distribution's own limit. Its quantile function saturates at the sample maximum, so it carries no information above about p = 1 − 1/n — 0.99 at n = 100. A handover that only starts at 0.99 leaves the graft relying on the empirical body across levels the empirical body cannot see, and the return-level curve flattens onto order statistics near the maximum long before the parametric tail is allowed to take over.

That gives a concrete design rule, and it is the mirror image of the one in section 7. The weight must not extend past where the data can speak; and the handover must complete before the empirical body runs out. With n observations, both point to the same place: finish the handover by roughly 1 − 2/n. At n = 100 that is 0.98, which is exactly where the best setting lands.

So the two weights should be decoupled, but not in the direction of pushing the handover later. The fitting weight can start anywhere the model is trustworthy; the handover is pinned near the top of the data by the sample size, not by the fit.

12Letting α depend on the level

Since the best α rises with the return period, the obvious next move is to let α depend on p. Does that still elicit anything?

Yes, and the argument is short. Properness here is a pointwise-in-p property. For each fixed level p, the mixed check function ραp is strictly consistent for the α-elastile at that level, because the expected loss is strictly convex in the prediction with a unique minimiser. Nothing in that argument cares whether the α used at level p is the same as the one used at level p′. So for any measurable schedule α(·), the criterion

R(θ) = ∫ w(p) E[ ρα(p)p(Y, T(p|θ)) ] dp

is bounded below by the sum of the pointwise minima, with equality exactly when T(p|θ) = Tα(p)(p; F) for w-almost every p. It is a strictly consistent scoring rule for the curve p ↦ Tα(p)(p; F). Fisher consistency survives too: under correct specification over the weighted region, the truth's curve is the model's curve, for any schedule.

Three things are worth saying about what you get.

The target is a hybrid. Different points on the elicited curve are different functionals of F — the 0.2-elastile at p = 0.9, the 0.8-elastile at p = 0.999. That is perfectly well defined but it no longer has a name like "the expectile function", and any theory you would want to import (asymptotic variance for expectile regression, say) does not transfer without redoing it.

Keep α(p) continuous. This is the one real constraint, and it is not about properness — it is about attainability. A model's quantile, expectile and elastile curves are all increasing in p. The target curve need not be. In the tail the expectile sits below the quantile, so raising α pulls the target down while raising p pushes it up. With any continuous schedule tested — α = p, a smoothstep ramp over [0.9, 0.999], even α = 1 − (1−p)0.05, which is above 0.7 by p = 0.5 — the target stayed strictly increasing, at ξ = 0.2 and at ξ = 0.45. A schedule that jumps (α = 0 below p = 0.99, 1 above) makes the target fall by 1.27 at the jump. The criterion is still proper there; it is simply aiming at a curve no model can match, which is misspecification you have manufactured for yourself.

It generalises further than α. The same pointwise argument licenses letting any parameter of the level-p loss vary with p — the scale s included — and it is also why the composite construction tolerates a different loss family at each level. The cost is always the same: more tuning surface, and oracle-selected schedules that need their selection cost charged before the reported gains mean anything.

13A separate GPD study: against what a practitioner would actually do

Every comparison so far has been against methods that fit one parametric distribution to the whole sample. Faced with a body as obviously non-GEV as this one, nobody competent would do that. They would pick a threshold, fit a GPD to the exceedances, and hard graft it onto an empirical body. That is the right competitor, and it deserves its own comparison rather than being mixed in with the GEV work — so no GEV method appears in this section, and every ratio is against POT–MLE at the 90th percentile, hard grafted.

The composite version is the natural analogue: fit a three-parameter GPD to the whole sample with a weight that rises from p = 0, then smooth graft it onto the empirical body using that same weight as the handover. Here, unlike the GEV case of section 11, tying the two weights together is the natural choice rather than a mistake — the composite weight already starts at zero on the body, which is exactly where the empirical distribution should be trusted, so the two jobs coincide.

One caveat on the truth

max(GEV, Normal) has a tail that is exactly GEV, and a GEV tail is only asymptotically GPD: S = 1 − e−z against z, a relative error of about z/2, so roughly 5% at the 90th percentile and 0.5% at the 99th. The GPD is therefore mildly misspecified for every method in this section, which is realistic and affects them all alike.

Threshold choice dominates the competitor

Before anything else: the practitioner's method is extremely sensitive to a choice it cannot make from the data. At T = 1000 the MSE of POT–MLE at thresholds 0.85, 0.90 and 0.95 is in the ratio 1.62 : 1.00 : 0.52 — a threefold spread from the threshold alone, with asymptotic biases of +20.6%, +8.8% and −1.7%. Switching from MLE to L-moments at the same threshold changes the MSE by a further factor of three. The composite estimator has no threshold; the weight plays that role, but it is a smooth choice rather than a discrete one.

Its asymptotic bias at T = 1000 is −0.5%, against +8.8% for POT–MLE(0.90) and +20.6% at the lower threshold.

Read the reference carefully

POT–MLE(0.90) is a weak yardstick in the far tail: at T = 1000 it is beaten even by the empirical distribution (0.23), which cannot extrapolate at all and simply returns the sample maximum. Its variance is what fails, not its centring. So "beats the reference at T = 1000" is a low bar, and the honest comparisons are against POT–MLE(0.95) at 0.52 and POT–L-moments at 0.32. The composite still wins those, and wins them on median error and win rate too, which the empirical does not — the empirical's 0.23 comes with a 27% win rate and the worst median error in the table.

Two secondary findings. The weight's shape matters more than where it ends: p⁶ beats p² beats smoothstep(p/0.8) at every return period. What works is a weight that rises from zero immediately — as proposed — but stays small across the body, so the criterion is dominated by the tail without ever being exactly blind to the rest. And L1 loses again: the composite quantile GPD is worse than its L2 counterpart everywhere and worse than the reference at T = 100, with an asymptotic bias of −25.9% at T = 1000. That is the reverse of the GEV case, where L1 was the asymptotically unbiased one, and it comes from the weight now covering the body, where the GPD cannot fit the contaminated shape and the pinball loss has no smoothing to fall back on.

Grafting matters here as much as it did for the GEV. Ungrafted, the composite L2 GPD carries eight times the reference's error at the 2-year level; grafted, 0.98. And this is the case where reusing the fitting weight as the handover is right: it starts at zero on the body by construction, so it hands the body to the empirical distribution automatically.

The elastile inside the GPD study

Sweeping α here reproduces the pattern of section 8, in the setting that matters most. The interior optimum is real at moderate return periods and the best α rises with T:

How much is left for a level-dependent alpha

Since the best α moves with T, the obvious next step is to let it move with p (section 12 shows that is proper). The ceiling is small: taking the best α separately at every return period — an oracle no schedule can beat — improves on the best single α (0.50) by 14% at the very far tail and 4.4% on average. That is the entire prize available, before any cost of choosing the schedule.

The other dial: La at a = 1.5

The exponent in the loss is a second, independent way to sit between L1 and L2. Rather than adding the two check functions, raise the residual to a power a between 1 and 2 — the La-quantiles. The two families share endpoints but are different curves in between: at p = 0.9 for GPD(0, 1, 0.2) the quantile is 2.925 and the expectile 2.875, while the 1.5-quantile is 2.747, outside the interval they span. So neither is a reparameterisation of the other and a result for one does not transfer. Run on the same 2000 replicates, against the same reference:

The exponent dial is dominated by the mixing dial. At every one of the six return periods the α = 0.5 elastile beats a = 1.5, and in the far tail pure L2 beats it too — 0.21 against 0.39 at T = 1000. What a = 1.5 does have is the most uniform win rate of anything here, never dropping below 0.65 at any return period where L1 falls to 0.52 and L2 to 0.62; it is the safest single choice if the return period of interest is unknown. But it is nobody's optimum.

A caveat that runs in a = 1.5's favour

The closed form used for the upper fractional moment needs ξ > 0, so the a = 1.5 fitter is constrained to positive shape and 14.2% of its fits sit pinned at that bound. The unconstrained fitters put 10–23% of their fits below zero, and since every fitter here underestimates ξ on average, censoring at zero prevents the worst underestimates rather than causing them. So the constraint flatters a = 1.5 — and it still loses to the elastile at every return period. Lifting it means integrating over the finite upper endpoint of a negative-shape GPD, which is straightforward but not done here.

Read with the moment conditions of section 7, this gives the two dials a clean division of labour. The exponent is the one that widens the domain — a = 1.5 keeps the root-n limit out to ξ < 1 where L2 stops at ξ < 1/2 — and buys little accuracy. The mixing weight buys the accuracy and widens nothing. For ξ = 0.325, comfortably inside both domains, there is no reason to reach for the exponent; for a tail heavy enough that L2 has no limit distribution, it is the only continuous route back to L1.

14Everything here is an M-estimator, and the elastile is an M-quantile

It is worth naming the framework these estimators already live in, because it supplies theory for free and it changes how the elastile should be positioned.

The estimators

Every composite estimator in this report minimises a sum over observations of a criterion in θ,

θ̂ = argmin Σ i ρ̃(y i; θ), ρ̃(y; θ) = ∫ w(p) ρ p(y, T(p|θ)) dp

which is exactly Huber's M-estimator with a particular ρ̃. Maximum likelihood is the case ρ̃ = −log f. (L-moments is not an M-estimator but is a Z-estimator, solving λ̂r = λr(θ), and the same asymptotics apply.)

The consequence is that standard M-estimation theory applies without modification. Under the usual conditions θ̂ is consistent for the population minimiser — the "asymptotic target" tabulated throughout this report — and asymptotically normal with the sandwich variance

V = A−1 B A−1, A = E[∇²ρ̃], B = Var[∇ρ̃]

Two things follow that would otherwise cost simulation. Analytic standard errors and asymptotic relative efficiencies, so the choice of weight and of α can be studied without a Monte Carlo at every setting. And a diagnosis of the near-flat ridge that dominates the variance in section 5: that ridge is A being close to singular over the tail-weighted region, which says the remedy is a reparameterisation or a penalty in that direction rather than a different loss.

How flat that ridge is, measured

Flat enough that the "asymptotic target" figures in this report are not converged at the sample size used to estimate them. Refitting the same criterion to three independent n = 5000 samples gives ξ̂ = 0.149, 0.233 and 0.405 for the one-sided M-quantile of section 15, and 0.213, 0.259 and 0.354 for pure L2 — a spread of a quarter in the shape parameter, at fifty times the sample size of the study. The three decimal places these targets are quoted to are therefore misleading, and comparisons between one estimator's asymptotic target and another's should not be read at that resolution. The 2000-replicate medians are the reliable summaries throughout, and the return-level results, which average over the ridge rather than sitting on it, are unaffected. This is the same near-singular A, seen from a different direction.

The functionals

The second sense of "M" is Breckling and Chambers' M-quantiles: the level-p M-quantile for an influence function ψ is the root of

E[ |p − I(Y < t)| ψ(Y − t) ] = 0

Every functional in this report is one of these, differing only in ψ:

The functionals as M-quantiles. The elastile row is verified against the definition to machine precision (residuals below 1e-11) in scripts/98-validate.R.
functionalψ(u)influencereference
Quantilesign(u)bounded—
ExpectileuunboundedNewey & Powell (1987)
La-quantile|u|a−1 sign(u)unbounded for a > 1Chen (1996); Daouia, Girard & Stupfler
α-elastile(2α/s) u + (1−α) sign(u)unbounded for α > 0this report, as an M-quantile
Huber M-quantilemin(k, max(−k, u))boundedBreckling & Chambers (1988)

So the α-elastile is not a new functional. It is the M-quantile with a linear-plus-sign influence function, and it sits inside a framework that is thirty-five years old. That is worth saying plainly, and it is not a loss: positioning it as "a particular M-quantile, chosen because its identification equation needs only the first partial moment" is both honest and stronger than claiming novelty, because it inherits the existing asymptotic theory rather than having to rebuild it. What is genuinely new here is the use — a tail-weighted composite criterion built on it, and the finding that the mixing parameter has an interior optimum that moves with the return period.

The robustness logic inverts

M-estimation exists to bound the influence of outliers, and by that standard the quantile (ψ bounded) is the robust choice and the expectile (ψ unbounded) the fragile one. Every result in this report points the other way: L2 has one-half to one-sixth of L1's far-tail error. The reason is that in tail estimation the "outliers" are the data — the large observations carry nearly all the information about ξ, and a bounded ψ deliberately discards it. Whatever is inherited from robust statistics, the usual advice about bounded influence should be inverted when the target is the tail.

The right word is tail-robustness, and there is prior art

Two literatures answer to "robust" here and only one of them is this one. The first applies classical robustness to extreme value models — Dupuis's optimal B-robust estimator for the GPD, and the minimum density power divergence estimator, which is indexed by a constant running from the MLE at zero to bounded influence above it. That family is structurally the elastile's twin — one dial from efficient to robust — but it runs the other way: it downweights large observations as contamination, where everything here upweights them as signal.

The second literature is the relevant one, and it is thinner. It calls the problem tail-robustness: contamination in the body corrupts the tail extrapolation, so weight the fit towards the tail. Fung's maximum weighted likelihood estimator (Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 107, 180–198, 2022; arXiv:2108.01356) proves the tail index remains consistent under model misspecification for a weighted likelihood, motivated by insurance claim severities rather than floods. That is prior art for this report's core claim, and the framing to adopt: saying "robust" unqualified invites the Dupuis/MDPDE reading and the objection that ψ here is unbounded. What is not in that work is the composite integration over levels rather than observations, the L2 and mixed-loss families, and the finite-sample accounting of section 16.

One caveat about which path to take between L1 and L2. The elastile and the La family share endpoints but are different curves: at p = 0.9 for GPD(0, 1, 0.2) the quantile is 2.925 and the expectile 2.875, while the 1.5-quantile is 2.747 — outside the interval they span. So the two are not reparameterisations of one another, and a result for one does not transfer to the other.

15Inverting the knot: capping the downside

If bounded influence is the wrong instinct here, the obvious move is to invert Huber's knot: constant influence where Huber is linear, linear influence where Huber is bounded. Two inversions are possible and they are not the same estimator.

(A) symmetric ψ(u) = sign(u) max(|u|, c) (B) one-sided ψ(u) = max(u, −c)

(A) bounds the influence of observations near the fitted level and lets it grow on both sides. (B) is what the argument above actually asks for: linear above the fitted level, capped below it, because it is the downside that carries the contaminated body. Both reduce to closed forms in the partial moment φ(x) = E[(Y − x)+] the earlier sections already provide, so neither needs quadrature:

(A) p [c S(t) + φ(t+c)] = (1−p) [c F(t) + (t−c) − m + φ(t−c)] (B) p φ(t) = (1−p) [c + φ(t) − φ(t−c)]

(B) is the interesting one, for a reason visible in the second line. The two mean terms cancel between φL(t) and φL(t−c), so its identification equation contains no model mean at all. Capping the downside removes the mean anchoring structurally, where section 10 had to substitute a noisy sample mean for it and lost at n = 100. Both closed forms were checked to 1e−13 against a kink-split reference quadrature at ξ = 0.1, 0.325 and 0.6. The limits hold exactly: (A) runs expectile → quantile as c goes 0 → ∞, non-monotonically, overshooting past the quantile near c = 10; (B) runs from the expectile (c → ∞) to a degenerate limit at the upper endpoint (c → 0), so it never reaches the quantile.

The contamination, measured honestly

A first pass showed (B) shedding all the body contamination at every level — better than the quantile, which would have been too good. It was. At c = 0.1 the nominal p = 0.90 functional sits at t = 11.29, which is the 0.99728 quantile: small c does not shed the contamination, it outruns it. Comparing at matched effective level F(t) instead:

k = 4 is the best far-tail estimator in this report. At T = 1000 it reaches 0.179 against a previous best of 0.209, and it beats pure L2 at every return period from T = 107 to 1000 with paired t between −5.8 and −12.5. Against the α = 0.5 elastile it wins at T = 529 and 1000 (t = −8.7 and −10.4), ties at 203 and loses at 107. The optimum is genuinely interior — k = 4 beats k = ∞, and the curve turns back up at k = 8 and 16 — so this is not "get as close to L2 as possible". It is also wide rather than a knife edge: even k = 16 still beats L2 at T = 1000 with t = −7.9.

Three qualifications, all against the derivation

The mechanism is not what wins. The theory predicted less bias. Finite-sample the bias is worse: −2.55 at T = 1000 for k = 4, against −1.94 for pure L2 and −0.76 for the elastile. It is more biased and wins on variance. At n = 100 the return-level bias is dominated by shape underestimation — median ξ̂ = 0.108 against a true 0.2 — which swamps the asymptotic contamination entirely.

The regime where the theory helps is the regime the data cannot support. Contamination vanishes at c ≤ 0.5, which is k = 0.25 to 0.5, and those give MSE ratios of 4.44 and 2.53 at T = 19. Section 7's third trap predicted it: at k = 0.25 fully 10.1% of the fitting weight lands above the largest observation, against 0.8% for pure L2, and the median fitted shape duly collapses to −0.176.

The useful regime is close to the expectile. Since k → ∞ is pure L2, k = 2 to 4 is a mild downside cap on L2, not the body immunity the population result advertised.

So the verdict is narrower than the derivation promised: a mild cap on the downside is the best far-tail estimator here, and the mean-anchoring argument that motivated it is not the reason. That is still worth having — the interior optimum is real, decisive and stable over a wide range of k — but it belongs in a paper as an empirical finding with a suggestive derivation attached, not as a theoretical result confirmed by simulation. The gap between the two is the same gap as between sections 3 and 10: an obstacle that is genuine asymptotically and invisible at the sample sizes flood frequency actually has.

16The honest test: when nothing is wrong

Every result so far is on a misspecified truth, where a tail-weighted criterion has misspecification to avoid. If the data really are iid from the fitted family, maximum likelihood is efficient and every estimator here is throwing information away on purpose. It should lose. The size of that loss is the insurance premium, and without it none of this is deployable.

An exactly correct GEV

iid GEV(0, 1, 0.2), n = 100, 2000 replicates, the weight starting at the median as section 5 recommends. The GEV MLE is now exactly right, so every ratio above one is what the method costs.

Three things. The body is where it hurts: every composite estimator is 2 to 3.7× the MLE's error at T = 2, which is the weight doing exactly what it was told to do in a setting where the body was informative. The far-tail premium is modest for two of them — 12% for the inverted Huber and 25% for the elastile at T = 1000, against 32% for pure L2. And L1 gets worse with return period rather than better, 1.11 at T = 48 rising to 2.83 at T = 1000: the variance explosion appears even with no misspecification to justify it, so L1 has no defensible regime here at all. L-moments meanwhile ties the MLE across the board, the known result at this sample size and a check that the harness is not flattering anything.

The bias runs the unsafe way

At T = 1000 the MLE is biased +1.01 and L-moments +0.45, while L2 is −1.52, the elastile −1.03 and the inverted Huber −1.93. The composite estimators under-predict the far tail, which for flood design is the dangerous direction. The cause is in the last column: median ξ̂ is 0.198 for the MLE against 0.095 for L2 and 0.085 for the inverted Huber, on a true 0.2. Tail-weighted fitting underestimates the shape badly at n = 100 even when the family is perfect, and a low shape shrinks the far-tail extrapolation.

An exactly correct GPD, done properly

The first version of this test drew from GPD(1, 0.5, 0.2) and fitted three parameters. That was wrong twice. A three-parameter GPD with unknown threshold is non-regular — the likelihood rises monotonically in μ up to min(y), so μ̂ is a boundary estimate — and, worse for the comparison, the reference was handed the true threshold while the composite estimators had to estimate it, so they were paying for a parameter the reference got free. A GPD used as a tail model has no location to estimate anyway: it starts at the threshold, and only scale and shape are unknown. So: iid GPD(0, 0.5, 0.2), μ known, two parameters for every method including the references, on a regular problem where the MLE is efficient.

Return periods need the exceedance rate

Here the GPD is the whole distribution, so exceedance probability 1/T is a T-year level and the labels below are self-consistent. Attached above a threshold with exceedance rate ζ, the T-year level solves ζ S(x) = 1/T, so a column labelled T is the (T/ζ)-year level: with ζ = 0.1 the column marked T = 100 is the 1000-year return level. No ratio changes — but the practically interesting range moves an order of magnitude left, into the middle of the table rather than its right edge.

The cost is confined to short return periods; there is no far-tail premium. Against the MLE — the figure's own reference — the one-sided estimator is 1.29 at T = 2 and 1.34 at T = 5, crosses below one by about T = 26, and reaches 0.633 at T = 1000: a 37% improvement on the efficient estimator with nothing misspecified at all. Against L-moments, the stiffer benchmark since it beats the MLE throughout, the same estimator runs 1.36, 1.35, 1.19, 0.98, 0.94, 0.91, 0.84, 0.76 across the columns, crossing below one at the same place. Both composite L2 and the elastile behave similarly but with a smaller far-tail gain. Under the ζ = 0.1 reading the crossing at T = 26 is the 260-year level, so the losing region is the lower part of the design range, not the whole of it.

What the short-return-period numbers were measuring

At T = 2 the four grafted fits give 1.284, 1.288, 1.283 and 1.289 against the MLE. Four completely different tail models returning the same number is the signature of the empirical body doing all the work, and the empirical distribution on its own gives 1.353 there. So that column is the empirical distribution's performance against a parametric fit, not the loss function's, and it should not be read as a cost of the composite criterion. It is a cost of grafting. The ungrafted GEV numbers above are a different matter — there is no empirical body in that study at all, so their 2–3.7× really is the weight discarding the body.

The bias still runs the unsafe way: at T = 1000, −0.69 for the inverted Huber and −0.44 for L2, against +0.23 for the MLE and +0.37 for L-moments. Median fitted ξ is 0.124 to 0.172 against a true 0.2.

What this does to section 13

Section 13 reports the composite L2 graft at an MSE ratio of 0.209 against POT–MLE(0.90) at T = 1000 on the contaminated truth. The identical comparison — same estimator, same three-parameter fit, same reference — with no misspecification at all gives 0.344. On a log scale that is 68% of the headline gain present with a perfect model, only 32% from the misspecification the method exists to exploit. The reference keeps ten exceedances out of a hundred observations. The result stands, but most of the margin is data efficiency, and the paper should say so rather than leave it to be extracted.

The recommendation. With no evidence of misspecification, use L-moments. On a correct GEV the composite estimators cost 12–32% in the far tail and 2–3.7× in the body; on a correct GPD they cost nothing in the far tail — the one-sided estimator reaches 0.63 against the MLE at T = 1000 — and the cost is confined to short return periods. The two studies disagree because the fitting setups differ, so neither number is the premium. In both, though, the estimators lean unsafe. What justifies them is the misspecified case, where they cut error by half to six-fold. The first question is not which loss to use but whether the body model is wrong — and section 2's argument is that for rain-on-snow, with an ordinary-snowmelt population sitting under a rain-driven tail, it usually is.

17What each estimator converges to above a threshold

Everything so far compares estimators at a fixed sample size. A cleaner question is what each converges to with unlimited data. Fit a GPD to exceedances over u = 3.16, the truth's 0.90-quantile, and every estimator has a pseudo-true limit: the GPD minimising its own population criterion against the truth's conditional law. Those limits differ, and the differences are the argument for the method with the sampling noise removed.

The natural target comes from threshold stability. If exceedances over u₀ are GPD(σ₀, ξ) then exceedances over any u ≥ u₀ are GPD(σ₀ + ξ(u − u₀), ξ): shape invariant, scale linear in the threshold. For a GEV(μ, σ, ξ) tail, S(x)/S(u) tends to a GPD with shape ξ and scale σ + ξ(u − μ) as u grows, so carrying that limit back to the threshold in use gives scale 1.6323, shape 0.2000. The construction checks out: the truth's conditional survival matches it to a maximum log-ratio of 9.7×10−3 at u = 6 and 2.7×10−7 at u = 100.

The limits, derived rather than simulated

Estimating these by fitting to a very large sample is not precise enough — the composite estimators separate by about as much as the seed-to-seed noise. They can be solved instead. Differentiating the composite criterion in θ, where the indicator contributes nothing because ρ is continuous at zero, the pseudo-true θ* solves

g pG(t) = E G[ |p − I(Y < t)| ψ(Y − t) ] = p E G[ψ(Y−t) I(Y>t)] + (1−p) E G[ψ(Y−t) I(Y<t)]

Write gpG for the M-quantile identification function of an arbitrary distribution G. The model's level-p functional Tp(θ) is defined by gpF θ(Tp(θ)) = 0. Then the pseudo-true θ* solves

∫₀¹ w(p) g pF(T p(θ)) ∇ θT p(θ) dp = 0 ∇ θT p(θ) = − [∂g pF θ/∂θ] / [∂g pF θ/∂t] at t = T p(θ)

The same function g appears twice, evaluated at two different distributions. At the model it defines the functional and, by implicit differentiation, its sensitivity. At the truth — the highlighted term — it measures the discrepancy: gpF(t) vanishes exactly when t is the truth's own level-p M-quantile. So θ* sets a weighted average of the level-by-level discrepancies to zero, weighted by w(p) and by the sensitivity. Two consequences follow at once: the target depends on the weight, and it depends on ψ only through which functional is being matched.

Everything is elementary once the truth's distribution function F and partial moments Φ̄(t) = E[(Y − t)+] and Φ(t) = E[(t − Y)+] are available, using Φ(t) = t − E[Y] + Φ̄(t) above the lower endpoint and Φ(t) = 0 below it:

quantile ψ(v) = sign(v) g p(t) = p − F(t) expectile ψ(v) = v g p(t) = p Φ̄(t) − (1−p) Φ(t) elastile ψ(v) = (2α/s)v + (1−α)sign(v) g p(t) = (2α/s)[p Φ̄ − (1−p)Φ] + (1−α)[p − F(t)] one-sided ψ(v) = max(v, −c) g p(t) = p Φ̄(t) − (1−p)[Φ(t) − Φ(t−c)]

For the composite quantile fitted to GPD(0, σ, ξ) exceedances the whole system collapses to something writable. With Tp = σ[(1−p)−ξ − 1]/ξ one has ∂T/∂σ = T/σ, and eliminating that equation from the second leaves the pair

∫₀¹ w(p) [p − F(T p)] T p dp = 0 ∫₀¹ w(p) [p − F(T p)] (1−p)−ξ log[1/(1−p)] dp = 0

two explicit integral equations in (σ, ξ). Solving them directly recovers (1.38035, 0.25484), the same root the general system gives, to five significant figures. For the expectile the model functional has no elementary form — it is the root of k φθ(t) + mθ − t = 0 with k = (2p−1)/(1−p) — but implicit differentiation of that equation still gives ∇θT in closed form, and it agrees with central differences to 2.5×10−10.

Solved to a residual below 10−10, with the two references obtained exactly as well (the likelihood limit minimises Kullback–Leibler divergence, the L-moment limit matches the first two L-moments):

Three things, and the first corrects an earlier claim in this report. Maximum likelihood and L-moments do not share a limit: 0.3459 against 0.3247 in shape. Under correct specification they would coincide, but under misspecification they target different functionals — a Kullback–Leibler projection and a moment match — and generically disagree. The gap is small next to their common distance from 0.2000, so on the figure they sit almost together, but there is no single "pseudo-true GPD" to speak of; each estimator has its own.

Second, ψ matters, but hardly at all among the losses with a linear part. The expectile, elastile and one-sided limits fall within 0.003 of each other in shape. The quantile sits 0.023 away, outside that cluster. So the meaningful division is between bounded and unbounded ψ, not among the unbounded ones.

Third, and most usefully, the weight moves the target monotonically towards the limit.

That is the theoretical justification the method needed. Concentrating the weight drives the pseudo-true target towards the limiting GPD, which is what a tail-weighted criterion is for; the finite-sample cost of concentrating it is the trap of section 7, and the tension between the two is what fixes a usable weight.

Matching expectiles helps even with no tail weighting at all

The m = 0 column is a flat weight — no tail focus whatever — and it still lands at shape 0.2637 against maximum likelihood's 0.3459. So roughly half the total movement from 0.346 to 0.200 comes from matching expectiles instead of maximising likelihood, before any weighting is applied. That is worth separating in a write-up, because it is a different argument from the one the method is usually sold on.

The limit is the right shape to aim at, not the right level

The carried-back limiting GPD is not the truth's conditional distribution, even asymptotically. Conditioning on X > u sweeps in the body mass the contamination adds at the threshold, so the ratio tends to a constant below one: Scond/Slimit → 1/[S(u)(1 + ξu/σ)1/ξ] = 0.8629, matched numerically to four decimals at x = 50, 200 and 1000. Equivalently the GEV component carries only 0.827 of the truth's survival at u. A POT fit is ultimately judged against the truth, so the limiting GPD is a target for the shape rather than the level, and the composite fits — converging on the limit — overshoot the truth in the far tail by about 15%, against maximum likelihood's factor of nearly three.

18The other way to tilt: weighting the likelihood

Section 16 closed on a question this report cannot dodge: if the point is tail-weighted fitting under misspecification, there is already a method for that. Fung's maximum weighted likelihood estimator (MWLE) does the tilting inside the likelihood rather than inside a loss, and it is the closest thing in the literature to what is being proposed here. It deserves to be run on the same data, not cited and left alone.

What MWLE is

Take a weight function w, non-decreasing, bounded away from zero and rising to one, and define a tilted density from the model density h:

f(y; θ) = h(y; θ) w(y) / C(θ), C(θ) = ∫ h(u; θ) w(u) du ℓ(θ) = Σ i w(y i) log h(y i; θ) − [Σ i w(y i)] log C(θ)

The normaliser is what makes this more than heuristic reweighting. Without it, weighting the log-likelihood is just a weighted M-estimator with no probabilistic meaning. With it, ℓ(θ) is a genuine log-likelihood — for the tilted family — so under misspecification the estimator converges to the Kullback–Leibler projection measured in the tilted metric. That is precisely a tail-weighted KL projection, and it is the same objective this report has been pursuing by other means.

Bridging the two weight functions

Fung's w acts on the raw value y; the weight used throughout this report acts on the probability level p. The two are made comparable through the quantile transform: set wFung(y) = ε + (1−ε) w(F̂(y)) with F̂ the empirical distribution function, and ε = 10−3 to meet the positivity requirement. The normaliser is then exact rather than quadrature: with y(1) < … < y(n) and wj = w(j/n) constant between consecutive order statistics, C(θ) = Σj=0n wj [H(y(j+1);θ) − H(y(j);θ)] with the endpoints at 0 and 1. Two checks: with w ≡ 1 the routine reproduces the ordinary MLE to five decimals in both families, and the exact C(θ) matches Monte Carlo integration of ∫hw.

MWLE takes the best far-tail number in the table — 0.86 at T = 1000, against 0.89 for the inverted Huber and 1.04 for pure L2 — and it recovers the shape better than anything else here, a median ξ̂ of 0.224 against a true 0.2 while maximum likelihood sits at 0.054. On the criterion that matters for extrapolation it is the strongest competitor this report has met.

It also has the worst body in the table by a factor of five: 32.5× the MLE at T = 2. The cause is structural. Fung's weight multiplies the density pointwise, so at w(p) = p6 floored at 10−3 the entire body contributes a thousandth of the tail's influence, and nothing in the objective pins the location. This is the same failure mode the composite estimators have — and it has the same repair, the graft of section 09.

Two reversals. Under contamination the composite estimators now edge ahead — 0.18 for the inverted Huber against MWLE's 0.23 at T = 1000 — and on correctly specified GPD data MWLE buys nothing at all: 0.99 to 1.03 from T = 200 outward, exactly the neutral result a tilted likelihood should give when the untilted one is already efficient, while the inverted Huber reaches 0.63.

Why grafting helps one and hurts the other

MWLE ungrafted has the smaller far-tail error of the two MWLE rows (1.03 against 1.41), which is the opposite of the pattern for every composite estimator, where grafting improves the tail as well as the body. The graft rescales the fitted survival function by its own value at the join, so it inherits the noise in S θ̂(u). For MWLE that quantity is badly determined: the weight multiplies the density pointwise and floors at 10−3, so essentially nothing in the objective constrains the fit near the 0.90-quantile, and the rescaling divides by a noisy number. The composite criterion, by contrast, still integrates over levels below the join with small but non-zero weight, and its fitted survival there is stable.

What to take from it

MWLE is the stronger method where the fitting problem is hard — the three-parameter GEV, where the shape is poorly identified and a tilted likelihood's efficiency is worth having. The composite estimators are stronger where the problem is regular — the two-parameter GPD above a known threshold, where a likelihood has no efficiency left to give away and what remains to be won is the choice of which discrepancy to minimise. Since the peaks-over-threshold setting is the one flood-frequency practice actually uses, that second regime is the one that matters for the application; but the GEV result is a real limitation and belongs in any honest account.

Where the composite construction still has ground

Three things survive the comparison. MWLE needs the model density in closed form and its normaliser integrated — here exactly, but not in general; the composite estimators need only the model's functional curve, which exists for families with no tractable density. MWLE inherits the likelihood's fragility when the family's support depends on θ, which is the GEV's usual numerical complaint. And its weight, acting on y, has no scale-free reading: w(p) = p6 means the same thing on any data, w(y) does not, which is why the bridge above had to run through F̂. None of that overturns the GEV efficiency comparison; all of it should appear alongside it.

19Does the handover have to be smooth?

Section 09 repairs the composite fit's body by blending it with an empirical body through the same weight w that defined the estimator. That is machinery: a mixture in the survival function, a derivative term, a numerical inversion. The simpler alternative is a hard graft — empirical below a join at the v-quantile, the fitted tail above, rescaled so the survival function is continuous:

Ŝ(x) = 1 − F̂n(x) x ≤ y (⌈vn⌉) Ŝ(x) = (1−v) S θ̂(x) / S θ̂(u) x > u = y (⌈vn⌉)

which is nothing but the standard peaks-over-threshold construction, and continuous by construction at the join. If that already fixes the body, the smooth handover is machinery without a purpose. The two were run on the same 2000 datasets and the same fitted parameters, so the only thing varying is the handover.

A hard graft is sufficient, and at v = 0.90 or 0.95 it beats this smooth graft at every return period in the table, including the far tail (0.16 against 0.18 at T = 1000). It is also brittle in the join: at v = 0.50 the same tail fit is 11× the POT–MLE at the five-year level, worse than not grafting at all, because a hard graft hands the model all of the probability above the join and a fit tuned for the 1000-year level has no business describing the five-year one. The smooth graft never does anything like that; its worst number anywhere is 1.49.

What this comparison cannot establish

It is tempting to read the table as hard beating smooth, and that reading is not available. Take the smooth graft's handover weight to the step w(p) = I(p > v) and, with the rescaling folded in, the smooth construction is the hard graft at v. The hard grafts are members of the same family, not a rival to it. What the run did was sweep the join over five values while holding the handover weight fixed at one — five members of a family against a sixth — and a family cannot be shown inferior to its own elements. The honest statement is narrower and still useful: w = p6 is a poor handover weight, and the reason is visible below. What a better one buys is a question for the graft work, not for this report.

Where the smooth graft's bump at T = 10 comes from

The green curve's one excursion above the hard grafts is at T ≈ 10, and it is the weight's own doing. The smooth graft gives the fitted tail a share w(p) of the blend, and w(p) = p6 at p = 0.9 is 0.531 — over half. So at the ten-year level the smooth graft is already majority-model, precisely where the model is worst relative to the empirical distribution, while a hard graft at v = 0.90 gives it exactly zero. The fix, if one wants smoothness, is a sharper weight for the handover than for the fitting; there is no reason the two have to be the same function, and this report used the same one only for tidiness.

One row deserves separate note. Every grafted estimator reads 0.98 at T = 2, identical to three decimals across five handovers and two tail models. That is not the tail model doing anything — it is the empirical distribution's own performance against POT–MLE(0.90) at the two-year level, which is what any graft must reduce to when the join sits above the point being predicted. The body number in every grafted table in this report should be read that way.

The practical answer, for now

Use a hard graft at the 0.90–0.95 quantile — not because hard handovers are better, but because it is the only setting in this family that has been tuned. Everything in this report that reports a grafted number uses w = p6 and is therefore reported against a handover that section 19 has just shown to be poor; the composite estimators' grafted results would improve, not degrade, under a better one.

The question the graft work should answer is not hard or smooth — that framing does not survive the nesting above — but which handover weight, and whether the optimum is interior. Three things point at an interior optimum: the hard graft's collapse at v = 0.50 shows the step is not uniformly good; its brittleness in v shows the criterion is not flat; and the smooth graft's single excursion sits exactly where the weight hands over too early. A handover family indexed from step to gradual, swept properly, is a small experiment and would settle it.

20Extremiles: the same idea in L-space

Every estimator so far has been an M-estimator: a functional defined implicitly as the root of an expectation. Extremiles (Daouia, Gijbels and Stupfler) are the other kind — an L-functional, defined explicitly as a weighted integral of the quantile function. They deserve a place here because they were built for exactly the purpose this report is about: a tail-sensitive location functional that is smoother than a quantile and reaches further than an expectile.

Fix τ ∈ (0,1) and set r(τ) = log(½)/log(τ), so r = 1 at τ = ½ and r → ∞ as τ → 1. The extremile is

ξ τ = ∫₀¹ J τ(t) q t dt, J τ(t) = r t r−1, r = r(τ)

and when r is an integer this is nothing but the expected maximum of r independent copies of Y, because r tr−1 is the density of the largest of r uniforms. That is the whole idea in one line: the τ-extremile of a daily series is the mean annual maximum when r = 365, and the reach into the tail is controlled by how many copies you take the maximum of, not by how far out a probability you name.

How it sits next to the others

The four families answer the same question — where is the distribution, seen from the tail? — with four different notions of "where".

Four ways to ask where a distribution sits, seen from the tail. The first three are M-functionals, defined as roots; the extremile is an L-functional, defined as an integral.
FamilyDefined byUsesTail reach
Quantile qpE[ p − I(Y<t) ] = 0one point of Fall of it, by fiat
Expectile epE[ |p − I(Y<t)| (Y−t) ] = 0partial meansneeds E|Y| < ∞
M-quantile (elastile, inv. Huber)E[ |p − I(Y<t)| ψ(Y−t) ] = 0partial ψ-meansset by ψ
Extremile ξτ∫ r tr−1qt dt, explicitall of F, polynomially reweightedneeds E|Y| < ∞

Two structural differences matter. First, the extremile is explicit: no root-finding, no estimating equation, and the sample version is a plain linear combination of order statistics with fixed weights — a probability-weighted moment with a tail-tilted kernel. Second, the extremile's weight is on probability, whereas ψ reweights on residual. The composite construction in this report already weights on probability; extremiles do it inside the functional as well, and stack the two.

Both model families have closed forms. For the GEV the derivation is one line: the maximum of r copies of GEV(μ, σ, ξ) is GEV(μ + σ(rξ−1)/ξ, σrξ, ξ), and taking its mean gives the result. For the GPD the integral is a Beta function.

GEV: ξ τ = μ + (σ/ξ) [ rξ Γ(1−ξ) − 1 ] GPD: ξ τ = μ + (σ/ξ) [ Γ(r+1) Γ(1−ξ) / Γ(r+1−ξ) − 1 ] (ξ < 1)

Both were checked against numerical integration of J τqt to better than 10−8, and the "expected maximum of r copies" reading was confirmed by simulation (r = 5, GEV(0,1,0.2): 3.0316 in closed form against 3.0304 from 2×106 draws).

What a composite extremile estimator can and cannot be

The composite estimators in this report all minimise a weighted integral of a loss. Extremiles have no such loss to integrate: they are L-functionals, and Newey–Powell-style asymmetric losses do not generate them. So the composite recipe does not transfer. What does transfer is the other half of the idea — matching a whole curve of functionals rather than a likelihood — as minimum-distance matching on the extremile function:

θ̂ = argmin θ ∫ w(τ) [ ξ̂ τ − ξ τ(θ) ]² dτ

with ξ̂τ = Σi [ (i/n)r − ((i−1)/n)r ] y(i) the empirical extremile. That is a tail-weighted probability-weighted-moment estimator, and its honest comparison is not the M-estimator family at all — it is Hosking and Wallis. L-moments match ∫Pk(t)qtdt for the first few shifted Legendre polynomials; this matches ∫r tr−1qtdt over a continuum of r. Same machinery, tail-tilted kernel.

The reach has to be an intermediate sequence

The obvious grid — run τ up to where r(τ) = n — produces an inconsistent estimator, and it took a while to see why. The empirical extremile at r = n puts weight 1 − (1−1/n)n ≈ 0.63 on the sample maximum alone, and the sample maximum is a badly biased estimate of E[max of n] for a heavy tail. Measuring that bias directly:

Relative bias of the empirical extremile against the truth, GPD(0, 0.6, 0.25), 20 000 replicates. At fixed r/n the bias does not shrink with n, which is why the reach must be capped by an intermediate sequence.
relative bias of ξ̂τr/n = 0.020.050.100.200.401.00
n = 100−0.001−0.008−0.025−0.037−0.071−0.149
n = 1000−0.003−0.009−0.018−0.028−0.056−0.129

The bias at fixed r/n does not shrink with n, so the reach must grow slower than the sample: rmax = αn with α → 0, the same intermediate-sequence condition (k → ∞, k/n → 0) that governs every tail-index estimator. With the cap in place the estimator converges: at n = 105, GPD(0, 0.6, 0.25) recovers (0.615, 0.246), and an α-sweep at n = 2×104 runs from (0.618, 0.243) at α = 0.01 to (0.683, 0.205) at α = 1 — the uncapped version's bias, visible.

At α = 0.02 the composite extremile costs nothing in the body — 0.98 at the two-year level, marginally better than the MLE rather than 1.9 to 2.0× worse — and still takes 26% off the far-tail MSE.
